lead: Logical effort is a pencil-and-paper method for finding the delay of a logic path and the transistor sizes that make it fastest. It splits each gate's delay into a part that depends on the gate's topology (its logical effort g and parasitic delay p) and a part that depends on its load (its electrical effort h). For a path with a fixed number of stages, delay is least when every stage bears the same effort, and that rule gives every gate's size in a few lines. Cell designers and synthesis tools use the same idea to choose drive strengths.
prereq: You need: propagation delay and how input capacitance grows with transistor width.

blocks.text: Measure delay in units of τ, the delay of an ideal inverter driving an identical inverter with no parasitic capacitance (about 3RC for a unit transistor of resistance R and gate capacitance C). Then the delay of a gate is:

blocks.where: h = C<sub>out</sub>/C<sub>in</sub> is the electrical effort (often called fan-out), g the logical effort, f = gh the stage effort and p the parasitic delay, all in units of τ or dimensionless.

blocks.text: Logical effort g is how much more input capacitance a gate needs than an inverter to deliver the same output current. Take a unit inverter with nMOS width 1 and pMOS width 2 (holes are about half as mobile), so its input capacitance is 3 units. A NAND2 has two nMOS in series, so each must be width 2 to match the inverter's pull-down, and its parallel pMOS stay at width 2: each input sees 2 + 2 = 4 units, so g = 4/3. A NOR2 has its two pMOS in series, each width 4, and nMOS of width 1: g = (4 + 1)/3 = 5/3.

Parasitic delay p is the delay from the gate's own diffusion capacitance, roughly proportional to the number of transistors on its output node. A fan-out-of-4 inverter (FO4) has d = 4 + 1 = 5τ; designers quote process speed in FO4 delays.

sections.h3: Path effort and the best stage effort

blocks.text: For a path of N stages, define the path logical effort G = g<sub>1</sub>g<sub>2</sub>…g<sub>N</sub> and the path electrical effort H = C<sub>load</sub>/C<sub>in,path</sub>. Where a node also drives gates off the path, its branching effort is b = (C<sub>on</sub> + C<sub>off</sub>)/C<sub>on</sub>, and B is the product of all b. The path effort is F = GBH.

The product of the stage efforts is fixed at F, so their sum is least when all are equal (the arithmetic mean is never below the geometric mean). That gives the best stage effort f̂ = F<sup>1/N</sup> and the least path delay:
D = N F1/N + P, P = p1 + … + pN Here d is the path delay in τ. P is added once, not once per stage on top of it.

The number of stages can be chosen too. D is smallest when the stage effort is about 4, so the best N is close to log<sub>4</sub> F. Adding inverters to a path that has too few stages makes it faster, even though each inverter adds its own delay.

items: Compute G, B, H and F = GBH; pick N (about log<sub>4</sub> F) and find f̂ = F<sup>1/N</sup>.
Start at the load and work back: each stage's input capacitance is C<sub>in</sub> = g × C<sub>out</sub>/f̂, where C<sub>out</sub> is what that stage drives.
Turn capacitance into widths: a gate whose input is k times its unit version gets every transistor k times wider.

blocks.text: This is often called path delay optimisation or the method of logical effort. It gives first-pass sizes; a timing tool then refines them with real wire loads.

examples.question: A path is inverter → NAND2 → inverter. Its input capacitance is C (a unit inverter) and it drives 64C. There is no branching. Find F, f̂, D and the input capacitance of each stage, and the transistor widths of the NAND2.
steps: Last inverter: C<sub>in3</sub> = 1 × 64C/4.403 = 14.54C. NAND2: C<sub>in2</sub> = (4/3) × 14.54C/4.403 = 4.40C. First inverter: C<sub>in1</sub> = 4.40C/4.403 = 1.00C, which matches the given input, a useful check.

Widths: a unit NAND2 input is 4 units (nMOS 2, pMOS 2) and C = 3 units, so 4.40C = 13.2 units, 3.30 times the unit NAND2. Each nMOS and pMOS is about 6.6 unit widths. The last inverter is 14.54 times a unit inverter: nMOS 14.5, pMOS 29.1.
Stage delays check: each stage has f = 4.40, so d = 5.40, 6.40 and 5.40τ, total 17.2τ.
examples.answer: D ≈ 17.2τ with input capacitances 1C, 4.40C and 14.54C (NAND2 transistors about 6.6 units wide, last inverter 14.5/29.1).

examples.question: A unit inverter (input C) must drive 64C through a chain of inverters. Compare N = 2, 3 and 4 stages.
steps: G = 1 and B = 1, so F = H = 64, and P = N.
log<sub>4</sub> 64 = 3, the stage count the rule predicts.
examples.answer: Three stages (sizes 1C, 4C, 16C) are fastest at 15τ; two stages give 18τ and four give 15.3τ.

traps: Writing f̂ = F/N. The best stage effort is the Nth root, F<sup>1/N</sup>.
Forgetting branching effort where a node also drives gates off the path; F comes out too small and the path looks faster than it is.
Inverting H. H = C<sub>load</sub>/C<sub>in,path</sub>, the output load over the path input.
Adding parasitic delay twice: D = NF<sup>1/N</sup> + P, with P counted once.
Giving every gate the same width. Equal effort means equal f, so the gates grow towards the load.

quiz.q: Define logical effort, electrical effort and parasitic delay.
quiz.a: g: input capacitance of a gate divided by that of an inverter giving the same output current. h = C<sub>out</sub>/C<sub>in</sub>. p: the delay of the gate driving no load, from its own diffusion capacitance, in units of τ.

quiz.q: Why is the logical effort of NOR2 larger than that of NAND2?
quiz.a: NOR2 has its pMOS in series. Each pMOS must be four units wide to match the inverter's pull-up, so each input sees 4 + 1 = 5 units (g = 5/3). NAND2 puts the cheaper nMOS in series and sees 2 + 2 = 4 units (g = 4/3).

quiz.q: An inverter drives 16 times its own input capacitance. Find its delay.
A path has G = 2, H = 32, B = 1, N = 4 and P = 5. Find F, f̂ and D.
A node drives 3C on the path and 1C off it. Find its branching effort.
A path has D = 20τ, N = 3 and P = 5. What stage effort does this imply, and what H if G = B = 1?
Why can adding two inverters to a two-stage path with F = 256 make it faster?
quiz.a: With N = 2, f̂ = 16 and D = 32 + P. With N = 4, f̂ = 4 and D = 16 + P + 2. The stage-effort saving of 16τ is far larger than the 2τ of extra parasitic delay.

beyond: Not for the exam. Synthesis tools pick drive strengths (X1, X2, X4 cells) and insert buffers using the same reasoning, with delay tables from the cell library instead of g and p. Logical effort also explains why wide gates are split into trees of NAND2 and NOR2. Search next for the book Logical Effort by Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, gate sizing and buffer insertion.
